Psychology in film, literature and music

Don Quixote and madness in literature

Cervantes created a lucid madman who has fascinated psychiatrists for four centuries.

Miguel de Cervantes tells us that Alonso Quijano, after reading so many books of chivalry, "from little sleep and much reading his brain dried up". He believes he is a knight errant, sees giants in windmills and armies in flocks of sheep.

A very sane madman

The fascinating part is that outside his chivalric obsession he reasons sensibly and gives wise advice, such as the counsel he offers Sancho before he governs his island. Many psychiatrists have tried to diagnose him over the centuries: monomania, delusional disorder, bipolar disorder. But he is a literary character, and those diagnoses say more about each era's psychiatry than about him.

The theory of the time, based on Huarte de San Juan's humours, put his state down to an excess of heat and dryness. At the end of the novel, Alonso Quijano regains his sanity and dies shortly afterwards, which has inspired many readings on the links between madness, imagination and freedom.

References

  1. Cervantes, M. de (1605–1615). El ingenioso hidalgo don Quijote de la Mancha.
  2. Iriarte, M. de (1948). El doctor Huarte de San Juan y su Examen de ingenios. CSIC.
